arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Mahoney argued the complaint alleged Domino's breached its contract with JWM.
She stated the complaint did not allege violations of McDonald's personal contracts.
Mr. Lichtenstein argued John McDonald forfeited his 1981 protection by choosing corporate ownership.
He contended section 1981 imposes a nondiscrimination duty outside contract law.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether federal anti-discrimination law protects individuals who own corporations. Domino's says corporate form changes the legal relationship. McDonald says the law protects the person, not just the entity.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Domino's wants the Court to rule that corporate ownership voids individual federal contract rights.
McDonald wants the Court to rule that federal law protects him personally despite his corporate structure.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Domino's argues that forming a corporation forfeits the individual's 1981 statutory protection.
McDonald argues that section 1981 imposes a nonnegotiable duty that ignores corporate form.

paragraphs: Justice Kennedy asked what damages the plaintiff sought in this specific case.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This dispute defines the scope of federal anti-discrimination protections for business owners. It determines whether corporate structures can shield companies from individual liability. The outcome shapes how small business owners access federal courts for contract disputes.
